item.title: Xi attends state dinner held by Trump
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-25
Xi attends state dinner held by Trump WASHINGTON -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Thursday evening attended a state dinner held by US President Donald Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the White House. Xi and Peng were warmly greeted by the US presidential couple upon their arrival. The two presidential couples posed for photos and met with guests attending the dinner. Xi and Trump delivered remarks respectively after the dinner began. Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes for the Mid-Autumn Festival to Americans from all sectors of society who care about and support the further growth of China-US relations. Xi noted that Trump paid a successful visit to China in May, and that the two heads of state exchanged state visits within six months, making history in bilateral engagement. He said common understanding on many issues have been reached during his visit this time, adding new substance to the constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, and providing fresh strategic guidance for bilateral ties. Xi stressed that over 200 years ago, soon after its independence, the United States turned its eyes to China. The two countries started trading with each other, exchanging goods to meet each other's needs and drawing on their complementary strengths. Noting that more than 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in the fight against Japanese militarist aggressors, Xi said such a friendship forged in blood and fire will surely live on through the generations. Over 50 years ago, Ping-Pong Diplomacy between the two countries reopened the door to bilateral exchanges that had been closed for years, Xi said. The older generation of Chinese and US statesmen, with the political wisdom of "a small ball moving the globe," set in motion the historic process of normalizing China-US relations. Xi said the story of an American named Ronald Sakolsky, who more than 20 years ago gave financial support to Chinese desert control worker Yin Yuzhen for her tree-planting effort, touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between the two peoples. Xi noted that bilateral exchanges have helped promote heart-to-heart communication between the two peoples and cemented public support for China-US friendship and cooperation. Today, China-US relations have come to another historical juncture, Xi said. Trump's pledge to make America great again and China's commitment to achieving great national rejuvenation are both ambitious goals that can surely be mutually reinforcing, he said. He said China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of the two peoples, keep pace with the trend of the times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other. Like a river that never stops flowing, history never stands still, Xi said, adding that the friendship between the two peoples is a worthy cause that holds great promise. The two sides should join hands and move forward side by side, nurture the beautiful flowers of China-US friendship, and write a new chapter in their friendly relations, he added. The state dinner was held in a warm and cordial atmosphere, featuring wonderful performances put on by American artists.

item.title: Public's view of China improving in the US
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-25
Public's view of China improving in the US Public attitude in the United States toward China has improved in recent times, with a growing number of US citizens favoring engagement with China over efforts to limit its growth, according to two major survey reports released ahead of Thursday's meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington, DC. A report released on Tuesday by the Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan organization, found that respondents gave China an average score of 37 on a zero-to-100 "feeling thermometer", where zero represented the "coldest" and most negative view and 100 the "warmest" and most positive view. The score is up from 28 recorded in 2021. The Pew survey was conducted from Sept 14 to Sunday among 5,193 US adults, including 1,168 who rated China. While people in the US continue to view China more negatively in general, the report showed that their attitude has improved in recent years. According to the poll, 19 percent of respondents now hold a positive view of China, up from 11 percent in 2021, while 27 percent have a neutral view, compared with 20 percent five years ago. Age played a key role in the survey. US adults under 50 gave China an average score of 42, compared with 31 among those aged 50 and older. However, both groups rated China more positively than they did in 2021. A separate survey report released on Monday by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs also found a shift from "containment" toward "engagement". The Chicago Council Survey, conducted from July 10 to 21 among a nationally representative sample of 2,156 adults, found that the respondents gave China an average score of 39, up from 26 in 2024. It is the highest level recorded by the council since 2020. The survey found that 57 percent of US respondents favored a policy of "friendly cooperation and engagement" with China, while 40 percent preferred actively limiting China's growth. Support for engagement has increased since 2024 and now extends across much of the political spectrum, the survey found. Perceptions of China have improved across partisan lines in the past two years, with both Democrats and Republicans viewing China more positively than before, the findings showed. The Chicago council also found that fewer people in the US now view China as a "critical threat". Forty-one percent said that China's territorial ambitions posed a critical threat to the US, down from 52 percent in 2022. The survey further found that people in the US are now more likely to say that China is earning global respect than they were in 2021. renali@chinadailyusa.com

item.title: What The Odyssey can teach China and US
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-25
What The Odyssey can teach China and US This summer, The Odyssey, a film directed by British filmmaker Christopher Nolan, became a global box office phenomenon. At a time when superhero films and established sci-fi franchises dominate the mainstream, a story based on Homer's epic, which was written nearly 3,000 years ago, once again captured audiences around the world. The discussion it sparked has gone far beyond the film itself. From war and peace to civilization and barbarism, people are using an ancient Greek story to revisit the problems confronting society today. Nolan has infused the ancient Greek myth with a distinctly modern set of values. The film is not merely about a hero's triumph over fate. It is the story of a veteran returning from war and confronting the violence, deception and collapse of trust that he himself helped create. US media have described Odysseus as carrying something akin to modern-day war trauma, turning his 10-year odyssey not merely into a journey home but also into a reckoning with his own moral choices. Embedded in the story are three lessons that remain highly relevant to society today: The first concerns the erosion of traditional virtues. The film repeatedly invokes a concept that is not explicitly articulated in Homer's original — Zeus's Law, which refers to the ancient code of hospitality under which strangers and hosts are expected to respect and protect one another. Nolan takes this ancient custom a step further, recasting it as a rule of modern civilization. People must believe in certain shared norms, he postulates, and even when dealing with strangers or potential competitors they must not cross certain lines. This is the foundation on which human societies form communities. Without this basic level of trust, people could not travel, trade, negotiate or build a stable social order. The tragedy at the heart of the film is that Odysseus himself, through his own ingenuity, violates precisely this rule. The Trojan Horse, one of the most famous stratagems in the history of warfare, becomes something more in Nolan's telling: an original sin of a moral kind. The second lesson concerns war itself. Traditional epics tend to celebrate how wars are won, but The Odyssey asks what happens after victory. Troy falls, and the Greeks win a glorious triumph, but the story does not end there. Agamemnon is murdered after returning home, Odysseus spends 10 years wandering, and the heroes of old are left dead, scattered or deeply scarred by what they have endured. The victors ultimately discover that conquering a city is not the same as winning a better world. The third lesson involves the crisis of trust created by the Trojan Horse. The stratagem that became a crucial turning point in the war was once widely celebrated as a triumph of human ingenuity, but the film reveals another side of cunning. From then on, any gift might be thought to conceal an enemy, and any act of trust might be exploited. The Trojan Horse was used only once, yet it was enough to make everyone who came afterward question whether the gates should ever be opened again. The horse thus comes to represent the "weaponization of trust": It destroys not only Troy, but also the very foundation that allows people to trust one another. These three lessons are not unfamiliar in today's China-US relationship. The two countries, first of all, need to develop a modern understanding of Zeus's Law in international relations. Even today, certain basic rules are needed to keep relations between major powers from breaking down: Nuclear weapons should not be used lightly; channels of communication should remain open during military crises; diplomatic commitments should not be overturned arbitrarily; economic and trade ties should not be weaponized without limit; and the other side's core security concerns should be taken seriously. These rules do not necessarily require the two sides to trust each other. They mean, rather, that even without trust, both sides know what must not be done. Genuine and durable stability between major powers rests on such rules. China and the United States likewise need to establish such understandings to prevent strategic rivalry from escalating without limit and to avoid the notion that undermining the other side's sense of security can somehow serve as a source of one's own security. The Odyssey reminds China and the US to guard against "competition without limits". The problem with the Trojan War was not simply the brutality of war itself; it is that when defeating the other side becomes the sole objective, the means used to achieve it can escalate beyond established boundaries. The scope of confrontation might expand, with sanctions and countermeasures piling up without end. Military deterrence can often be just one step away from an accidental clash. Each individual escalation may appear rational and justified on its own, but taken together they can push both sides toward an outcome that is anything but rational. The Odyssey also offers a more immediate warning: how to deal with the Trojan Horse problem. Modern states, of course, cannot afford to be complacent about security risks. Chips, communications, artificial intelligence, data, finance and critical infrastructure all have security implications, and neither China nor the US can afford to abandon safeguards altogether. But when the logic of security expands without limit, normal interactions can be interpreted as infiltration, scientific cooperation as technology theft, people-to-people exchanges as intelligence activity, corporate investment as strategic control and supply chain dependence as a security vulnerability. A dangerous cycle can then emerge: The more the two sides fear Trojan Horses, the more they guard against each other, reduce normal exchanges and weaken mutual understanding. In turn, the less they understand each other, the more readily they may interpret everything the other side does as a potential Trojan Horse, causing the security dilemma to reinforce itself. Power makes people believe they can defeat their opponents; fear makes them suspicious of every stranger and cleverness makes them believe that rules can be temporarily set aside. What is truly difficult is exercising restraint and rebuilding rules and trust. In May, when the Chinese and US leaders met in Beijing, they proposed building a "constructive relationship of strategic stability", seeking to address precisely these challenges and bring bilateral ties back to a level at which cooperation is the mainstay, competition stays within bounds, differences remain under control and the prospect of peace grows. For China and the US, the ultimate measure of strategic success is not victory or defeat. The real test for both countries is whether they can prove that humanity is capable of breaking free from the cycle of history and forging a new path for human civilization. The author is an assistant research professor at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations. item.title: Chinese, US first ladies visit National Museum of Asian Art
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-25
Chinese, US first ladies visit National Museum of Asian Art WASHINGTON -- Peng Liyuan, wife of Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Melania Trump, wife of US President Donald Trump, visited the National Museum of Asian Art in Washington on Thursday. Peng and Melania visited exhibition halls including the Peacock Room. Peng expressed appreciation for the US side's return of Chinese cultural relics to China on multiple occasions in recent years, expressing hope that China and the United States would continue to strengthen cooperation on cultural exchanges and cultural heritage protection, and deepen the friendship between the two peoples. After the tour, Peng and Melania watched American teenagers sing Chinese songs together and had cordial exchanges with them. Peng encouraged them to continue studying the Chinese language and culture and to become envoys of friendship between China and the United States. The National Museum of Asian Art is a renowned US institution dedicated to the collection, research and exhibition of Asian art.
